items.title: 67460_Sammy Price oral history interview
items.q: I made those records that /I made with Cousin Joe and Socks Wilson, and Coot Grant and Hot Lips Page, and then I made a series of things, "Step Down, Step Up," and "133" and all that.

ctx.x: They had a family band, yeah. A family band in Okmulgee, Oklahoma. And that's when I first saw him. And then I met Walter Page. Walter Page and Willie Lewis had the Blue Devils and they had a good band. Hot Lips Page later joined them in Tulsa. And then I just became ......., but I was playing more and more... not for money. I used to just play and give the money to the other person. If they would say, 'it's bad and we want you to play tonight, will you help us out?' 'Yeah.' They'd have seven, eight…

band. And you know, Budd Johnson and Buster Smith, Dad Minor—I don't know if you know who Dad Minor is, he's a trombone player ...Dan Minor and John R. Davis and Willie Owens...these were all local lights, but they were well known. Like you had another segment in Dallas, like Troy Floyd and Benny Long and people like that who went with Trent, and Benno Kennedy and these musicians...

items.title: 67460_Sammy Price oral history interview
items.q: I also said it was very common to see ... Lips Page ... because he was a prolific writer and, you know what I mean, was a great guy.

ctx.x: You know, when I told you that I went to, you know... from Oklahoma City to Kansas City, and then I said that Kansas City had become the jazz capital overnight, and I also said it was very common to see Louis Armstrong, Count Basie, Vic Dickenson, Lester Young, Walter Page, Lips Page, Jack Washington, Jimmy Rushing, Big Joe Turner, Julia Lee, Bennie Moten, Eddie Durham, who was a factor, and a tremendous factor in the total structure of those territorial bands, because he was a prolific writer and, you know what…
